paras: The lynching of Slume and Jonninna was the hanging of two Kootenai men by a party of white settlers on the east bank of the Flathead River, opposite Demersville in Missoula County, Montana Territory, in March 1888. The settlers accused the two, with a third Kootenai named Antley who escaped, of killing three prospectors on Wolf Creek the previous summer. The hanging set off a scare of a Kootenai uprising, a petition for federal troops and wire coverage across the country.

In mid-March 1888, Sheldon correspondents of the Missoulian reported that settlers had learned of the killing of three men on Wolf prairie, about 50 miles from Ashley, the previous June, and were arming to pursue the Kootenais accused of it. Versions of that killing differed on how many Kootenais took part, from three to about ten, though all said the prospectors were shot. A Thompson Falls correspondent suggested the dead were Ben Thompkins, one Johnson and Daniel McDonald, missing since leaving Libby on July 1, 1887.

According to Charles V. Jones, whose account the Daily Yellowstone Journal printed, about eighty men set out early one morning from Ramsdall's store and seized Slume and Jonninna at a Kootenai camp while they slept. The Missoulian put the party at forty-five to fifty settlers and said an Indian rider warned Antley, who fled. Wire reports said the two had been arrested on a warrant and placed with a deputy sheriff, and that citizens took them from his guard in his absence; Jones said the settlers retook them after the deputy at Demarsville had handcuffed them.

The prisoners were taken across the Flathead River into the timber, where, in Jones's telling, an Indian boy testified through interpreters and Slume confessed in English. The Missoulian wrote that the settlers "resolved to hang the two Indians, instead of turning them over to the law and its uncertain results." With one rope, they hanged Jonninna and then Slume from a tree limb, and later buried the bodies.

Fear of reprisal followed: settler families gathered at G. M. Lakin's, the Sheldon schoolhouse and Ashley, and armed squads guarded the crossings. A mass meeting at Ashley on March 25 named a committee to petition the Secretary of War for troops. Settlers then met Chief Eneas, who, according to a Sheldon correspondent, said he was satisfied with the hanging and would give up Antley if caught.

Reporting to Maj. Gen. Ruger from Arlee on April 22, Indian Agent Kenan wrote that citizens "did execute two Kootenai Indians some time last month" and that he believed the murder charge true. He said the settlers' leader, one Ramsdale, had told Eneas of the hanging, and that Eneas regretted the settlers had taken the law into their own hands. No report of an inquest or of arrests of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

Montana papers treated the dead as guilty, under headlines such as "Hi Yu Skookum!" and "Two of the Three Kootenai Devils Swung From a Tree by Settlers." The Missoulian called the men "bad Indians" whose deaths caused "little if any mourning," and a Minnesota digest said the settlers had "made good Indians" of them.

Elsewhere the story ran as brief wires datelined Ashley or Helena, under headings like "Indians Lynched" and "Indian Troubles," from Los Angeles and Fort Worth to Arizona and Dakota. These stressed fear of an outbreak, and one later digest said three Kootenais had been hanged.

A few papers dissented: the New York Sun asked whether the settlers had lynched innocent men, and the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner said the law would have better prevented revenge. The Philipsburg Mail, while thinking the men probably guilty, called for an investigation.

An Ashley wire put the lynching on "the 31st instant" and a Helena wire of April 3 said "to-day," but a settler's letter describing it had reached Helena before March 27. The local evidence points to mid-March: Jones dated the settlers' move three weeks before April 6, and an Ashley dispatch of April 11 gave March 19. The party's size was given as forty-five to about eighty, and the place as Demersville, Penny's mill or Ashley, the last a dateline.

accounts.label: Ashley wire
accounts.gist: Two Kootenais arrested and held by a deputy were taken from his guard by fifty citizens and lynched on 'the 31st instant'; trouble feared.

accounts.label: Settler's letter from Lakin's
accounts.gist: Families had gathered for safety after 'the lynching of two Indian murderers at Penny's mill'; the Kootenais were understood to have taken the warpath.

accounts.label: Charles V. Jones (Daily Yellowstone Journal)
accounts.gist: About eighty men from Ramsdall's store seized Slume and Jonninna; a deputy at Demarsville took and handcuffed them; the settlers retook them, held a 'trial' with an Indian boy as witness, and hanged them one at a time.

accounts.label: Missoulian
accounts.gist: Forty-five to fifty settlers from Demersville seized the two at their lodges, rowed them across the river and hanged them on the east bank, then buried them; no deputy is mentioned.

accounts.label: Indian agent's report
accounts.gist: Citizens executed two Kootenais 'some time last month'; the agent believed the murder charge true and blamed a white traveler's false alarm for the scare.

framing.detail: Montana headlines 'Hi Yu Skookum!' and 'Two of the Three Kootenai Devils Swung From a Tree by Settlers' and the line that the dead were 'bad Indians' whose deaths caused 'little if any mourning'.
The Minnesota digest 'Lynching Bad Indians' said the settlers had 'made good Indians' of the prisoners.
Out-of-territory papers ran brief Ashley or Helena wires under 'Indians Lynched' or 'Indian Troubles', stressing fear of an outbreak.
The New York Sun asked whether the settlers lynched innocent men and said the resulting alarm outweighed any satisfaction from revenge.
The Butte Miner said the law would have been the more effectual course, and the Philipsburg Mail, while thinking the men probably guilty, called for an investigation.
